name: Horseshoe Lake · Woodland park bank
description: An easy still-water trout option with a long public park bank and room to spread out. The open lawn and shoreline path leave anglers visible to other park users.

scoreReasons.bankQuantity: WDFW describes ample bank access; satellite shows an extended open city-park shore.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: The selected grass/rock edge gives a clear casting position without needing a dock.
scoreReasons.accessEase: Marked park parking and a short, nearly level route are visible.
scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The maintained north-bank rock edge directly fronts the park's open lawn and shoreline path. There is room to spread out, but walkers and people using the lawn or parking area can readily see an angler.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: Still lake water and a no-wake setting suit beginner bait and spinner fishing.
scoreReasons.scenery: Lake and park greenery are pleasant; road and town infrastructure are prominent.
scoreReasons.evidence: Official fishery, city park, current-year stocking and direct satellite inspection agree.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Winter and spring trout plants produce the strongest bank opportunity. Summer warmth reduces shallow trout activity, with crappie and perch providing alternatives. Autumn cooling improves trout feeding. The curve assumes ordinary legal park access and follows the regular fishery cycle.

name: Lake Sacajawea · Martin's Dock shore
description: An urban trout lake with a long public walking loop. The selected promenade at Martin's Dock has room to fish and frequent opportunities to be seen from the path and open lawn.

scoreReasons.bankQuantity: Long public park shoreline and multiple access points offer alternatives when one position is occupied.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Concrete promenade/projection and open nearby bank provide workable casting.
scoreReasons.accessEase: Walk west across the park lawn/path to the lakeside promenade, about 120 m. Keep the public path clear while casting.
scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The selected promenade at Martin's Dock sits directly beside the public lake loop, open lawn and recreation area. Anglers can space out around the lake, but walkers have clear views of this position.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: Still-water shore fishing fits bait/bobber and spinners.
scoreReasons.scenery: Trees, bridges and landscaped waterfront make an attractive urban setting.
scoreReasons.evidence: Official park and stocking evidence, mapped route and a dated advisory-lift report support the assessment.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Agency guidance describes rainbow and brown-trout stocking January-May, plus late-winter broodstock. Those months lead the curve. Warm summer water lowers trout prospects; warmwater fish provide a secondary summer opportunity. Cooler autumn water gives a moderate holdover fishery before the winter cycle.

name: Silver Lake · resort day-access docks
description: A verified paid way to reach Silver Lake's fishable docks. Crappie and perch are credible targets, but limited dock space and parking make this a weak match for bank fishing's separation requirement.

scoreReasons.bankQuantity: WDFW rates general shore access poor; this resort supplies a limited dock footprint.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Docks reach open water and avoid dense shoreline vegetation.
scoreReasons.accessEase: Check in at the resort office and pay for day access before walking past the waterfront building onto the dock. Use the visitor parking assigned by staff.
scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The main fishing dock is reached past the waterfront building and remains exposed to resort visitors and other anglers. Its shared deck offers little physical separation or visual screening when occupied.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: The dock reaches still lake water suited to a float, small jig or bait presentation.
scoreReasons.scenery: Lake and wooded shoreline are attractive, with resort structures nearby.
scoreReasons.evidence: Agency fishery assessment, operator's public day-pass terms and directly viewed docks are consistent.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Crappie and perch are the main accepted targets. Spring warming and the fall crappie period favor small jigs or bait around dock structure. Cold winter fish are less active and often farther from shore. The historical resort report supports a September-early December pattern, with October a strong ordinary month.

name: Wallace Pond · South Lewis County Park
description: A small, regularly stocked trout pond with gentle water, multiple piers and open-bank alternatives. Public daylight access; historical summer algae blooms and limited recent testing are detailed below.

scoreReasons.bankQuantity: County confirms several piers and a pond trail; imagery shows additional open bank.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Selected open bank has lawn behind it and direct still-water casting.
scoreReasons.accessEase: From the south lot, follow the paved pond-side path northeast, then step onto the open grass bank. About 60 m, mostly level.
scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The selected grass bank is between the pond and its paved loop path. It provides easy spacing along the shore, but walkers and nearby park users have a direct view of the fishing position.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: Small sheltered still-water pond is an excellent match for a beginner setup.
scoreReasons.scenery: Parkland between the pond and Cowlitz River offers a pleasant setting.
scoreReasons.evidence: Official access and stocking are well supported. The October 27 review found no current advisory and established daylight access. Recent toxin measurements remain unavailable, so research confidence stays 6/10; suitability scores do not take a documentation penalty.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: This small pond receives substantial catchable-trout plants. Winter and spring stocking create strong bank periods; the established late-fall stocking program supports November-December. Summer heat reduces trout activity, while autumn cooling improves feeding. Actual delivery dates can change the best week within a month.

name: Mayfield Lake · Ike Kinswa day use
description: A forested reservoir access with a fishing dock, several bank openings and a substantial rainbow-trout stocking program. It is a good keeper candidate when the chosen bank has room.

scoreReasons.bankQuantity: WDFW identifies fair bank access at the park; much of the reservoir's total shore is not practical public bank.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Day-use fishing dock and adjoining open park shore reach fishable water outside the roped swimming beach.
scoreReasons.accessEase: Walk west from the day-use lot through the public picnic area to the small shore opening north of the swimming beach. About 200 m. Stay outside the swim enclosure.
scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The small bank opening north of the swimming beach has forest around parts of its approach. Picnic users, swimmers and boats can still see the opening, and the nearby dock concentrates anglers.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: The selected sheltered reservoir edge has still water suited to bait, floats and spinners.
scoreReasons.scenery: Forested reservoir arms and parkland provide a strong scenic fit.
scoreReasons.evidence: Official state park and fishery pages, rules, current-year plant mirrors and satellite all support the baseline; exact recent bank catch success is less certain.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Repeated spring and summer rainbow plants sustain the fishery into late summer. Spring and early summer offer the strongest ordinary bank prospects; summer heat moves some trout deeper. Fall cooling supports renewed shore feeding. Winter remains fishable with a slower bite.

name: Cowlitz River · Mission / Massey Bar

name: Henry Hagg Lake · Sain Creek
description: Scenic reservoir cove with a real parking lot and room to spread out. The strongest fresh trout evidence in this Oregon seed set, tempered by a substantial autumn drawdown.

scoreReasons.bankQuantity: Inference: the cove and connected shoreline offer more room than a single dock; actual usable bank changes with reservoir level.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Open casting areas and connected shore support good bank fishing. The October 21 report of 28% reservoir storage makes extra uneven walking plausible; current mud and the exact waterline were not observed.
scoreReasons.accessEase: From Sain Creek parking, cross the picnic lawn southeast to the open shore below the shelter. Continue toward the water only on firm exposed bank as the reservoir drops.
scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The selected Sain Creek shore is below the picnic lawn and pavilion with a largely open approach to the water. The cove allows anglers to spread out, but picnickers, people crossing the lawn and lake users can readily see this position.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: Inference: still cove water suits bait and spinners; wind and occasional boat wakes are the main disturbance.
scoreReasons.scenery: Inference: wooded hills, cove views and forest trails fit an angler well.
scoreReasons.evidence: Inference: owner access, regulations, fresh stocking schedule, dated level report and satellite layout align; exact current casting waterline remains variable.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Judgment from recurring trout plants and documented warmwater seasons. Spring offers trout plus shallow-water smallmouth and panfish. Summer trout retreat deeper; accepted warmwater species sustain the cove. Autumn cooling and fall plants restore strong trout prospects. Reservoir drawdown can change this specific shore approach.

description: A strong stocked-trout fishery in a wooded basin, with a shared pier and limited bank openings. an angler's full-lot experience makes parking and personal space important obstacles.

scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Spring stocked trout make March-May the useful window, with an April peak around documented planting. Shallow water and vegetation constrain the later trout season. Resident crappie provide a limited alternative; a consistent useful-size autumn catch is less well supported.

name: Swofford Pond · northeast bank
waterSpeedNote: Still water at the selected bank. Wind can add surface chop.

scoreReasons.waterManageability: Sheltered lake-edge water is easy to control in ordinary wind, though weeds and shallows affect placement.
scoreReasons.scenery: Open wetlands and island vegetation offer an attractive natural setting.
scoreReasons.evidence: Historical agency bank guidance, current rules and aerial layout align; species inventory is secondary and current shoreline depth is unresolved.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Wildlife-area access is closed October 1-April 15. April rates only its open days. Crappie and perch prospects improve in warming spring and early summer water, then decline as shallow water becomes weedy and cools.

name: Steamboat Landing Park · public fishing dock
waterSpeedNote: The dock is exposed to Columbia flow, wind and wakes. A weighted bait or lure can be worked near the edge in calmer conditions; a light float can drift out of the useful zone.
description: A public fishing dock with a short boardwalk approach. Smallmouth and seasonal hatchery coho are the main targets. Deck space is shared, and Columbia current, wind and wakes affect bait and lure control.

scoreReasons.accessEase: Public off-street parking and connected gangways provide a short approach. The city lists ADA access.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: The dock is exposed to Columbia flow, wind and wakes. A weighted bait or lure can be worked near the edge in calmer conditions; a light float can drift out of the useful zone.
scoreReasons.scenery: Broad river views and the Gorge entrance give the dock a strong setting.
scoreReasons.evidence: City fishing permission, dock construction dimensions and inspected aerial layout agree. Recent bank catch rates and live dock occupancy remain unknown.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Smallmouth shoreline activity generally improves as water warms in spring and is strongest from late spring through early fall. Cooler late-autumn water lowers the expected bank bite. Fall hatchery coho provide a separate, run-dependent opportunity. These monthly scores are a seasonal judgment, not a catch forecast.

retentionNotes: October through December in the open lower North Fork: salmon 6/day, up to 3 adults with at most 1 adult Chinook; retain Chinook and hatchery coho only. Trout 2/day, minimum 14 inches; hatchery steelhead 3/day, minimum 20 inches. Release protected wild fish and follow catch-record requirements. This Colvin Creek-to-powerline reach is open June 1-October 31 and December 16-April 30. Anti-snagging and night-closure rules apply April and June-October. Water above the powerlines is closed. Salmon minimum size is 12 inches. The 2026 guide requires the Columbia River Salmon and Steelhead Endorsement when targeting those fish.
seasonNotes: Fall salmon and winter hatchery steelhead provide the main meal-size opportunities. Spring Chinook and summer steelhead create additional windows. crowdNotes: Run-time anglers and boat launches share a limited lower bank. Space improves outside peak weekend hours.
unknowns: Dam releases can make the selected slower margin unsuitable for a float on a particular day.

name: Swift Power Canal · fishing pier and upstream bank
waterSpeedNote: A broad slow-moving canal supports bottom bait and controlled float fishing. Generation changes can strengthen the drift; this is not a rushing natural river.
description: A stocked, bank-only trout fishery with an accessible pier and long open canal banks. One of the clearest practical additions for bait and spinner fishing.

scoreReasons.seclusion: Privacy judgment: The pinned fishing platform is beside the road bridge and parking, fully visible to arriving anglers and passing users. The long upstream bank adds physical room, but the platform itself provides little screening.

scoreReasons.bankQuality: Open banks and a clear pier edge permit straightforward casting.
scoreReasons.accessEase: Small roadside parking by the pier offers a short, level approach; farther bank positions require a gravel walk.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: A broad slow-moving canal supports bottom bait and controlled float fishing. Generation changes can strengthen the drift; this is not a rushing natural river.
scoreReasons.scenery: Forested mountains surround a visibly engineered channel.
scoreReasons.evidence: Official stocking and reach rules combine with a specific pier guide and direct aerial inspection.

name: Kalama River · Fisherman's Loop

sources.title: Cowlitz River · Wallace Bar easement access
sources.supports: Official public water access, access facilities and mapped location. I-5 to Exit 57. W on Barnes Dr and continue straight onto Rogers Rd. After 2 mi, R on Mandy Rd. After 0.5 mi, L into Wallace Rock Products and follow Public Fishing signs to parking lot. Follow gravel walkway to the streambank. This WDFW access area is on private property. Please respect the landowners by remaining within the WDFW-managed area. A detailed map is provided at the link above. The access area consists of a parking lot, designated driveway to and from Mandy Road, and a 25' strip of land bordering and extending nearly two miles along the bank of the Cowlitz River. Public use is limited to pedestrian travel and/or sport fishing only in the streambank area shown on the map, the upper portion extending 3,500' upstream of the parking lot and the lower portion downstream 6,900' to the county line. The lake adjacent to the parking lot is NOT open to the public.

waterSpeedNote: The bank edge can support a short controlled drift. The main run has enough current that a fixed bobber is a poor choice after rain.

scoreReasons.scenery: Forested slopes and river views make the bank scenic, with the road or access structures still visible.

name: Washougal River · Three Mile / Cottrell Dam bank
waterSpeedNote: The chosen pool margin is slow enough for a float or spinner. The rapid at either end and high-water conditions require a different assessment.
description: A deep roadside pool with a real gravel bank and room to spread out below the steep entry.

scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The wooded steep approach offers useful screening from the road, and the gravel shelf has room to separate from a few anglers. The fishing edge remains exposed to other users of the same shelf and swimming pool.
scoreReasons.bankQuantity: The managed parcel includes a substantial gravel opening, with wooded slopes limiting the rest.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: The selected opening provides room for a conventional cast. Trees and uneven shore limit some casting angles.
scoreReasons.accessEase: The documented bank access has a steep descent and a tree-covered parking approach.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: The chosen pool margin is slow enough for a float or spinner. The rapid at either end and high-water conditions require a different assessment.
scoreReasons.scenery: Forested slopes, river views and the Gorge landscape make this an attractive place to spend time.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Fall hatchery salmon and winter hatchery steelhead support the main keeper periods. Ordinary trout must reach 14 inches, which limits casual trout success. The monthly profile reflects these seasons; March and May have partial-season restrictions.
scoreReasons.evidence: Official access and fishing rules were cross-checked with inspected aerial imagery. Fish prospects are a judgment from the listed fishery evidence, separate from this confidence score.

name: Rood Bridge Park ramp
waterSpeedNote: Slow near-bank drift is inferred at the selected access. This describes the fishing margin; stronger flow farther out is not a second water-speed category.
description: A quiet wooded bend with a compact paved ramp. Crappie provide the main keeper chance; the park's large footprint does not mean continuous open riverbank.

scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The launch is immediately beside Rood Bridge and a small river parking area. Vegetation screens the wider park, but launch users, nearby bridge users, and paddlers can see the compact ramp margin directly.
scoreReasons.bankQuantity: One compact ramp opening supplies the useful bank, despite the larger park.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Open casting lanes exist at the chosen entry; the description identifies vegetation and footing limits.
scoreReasons.accessEase: From the small river lot, follow the paved path about 100 feet downhill to the concrete launch. Use a dry edge and keep boat access open.

name: King City Community Park dock
waterSpeedNote: Slow near-bank drift is inferred at the selected access. This describes the fishing margin; stronger flow farther out is not a second water-speed category.
description: A small fixed dock beside a slow, tree-lined reach of the Tualatin. It is an easy water choice once you get down the steeper approach.

scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The river trees offer some screening from the surrounding neighborhood, but the approach follows an open utility corridor to a small shared dock. Visitors on that path and people on the river can see the fishing position, and another party would occupy much of its usable space.
scoreReasons.bankQuantity: The dock is the main usable fishing area; most nearby bank is vegetated.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Open casting lanes exist at the chosen entry; the description identifies vegetation and footing limits.
scoreReasons.accessEase: From the gravel parking strip beside the park, follow the dirt path under the power lines to the small river dock, about 400 feet. The dock floods seasonally; use it only when dry and open.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: At this near-bank position, a light weighted rig or float should remain controllable in ordinary flows. Boat wakes and high runoff can change that.
scoreReasons.scenery: The rating reflects the visible river, trees and surrounding development.
scoreReasons.evidence: Manager access information, the fishing inventory and inspected imagery support this candidate. Its scores remain judgments that can change with experience.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Spring and fall can draw crappie into reachable cover and support useful bank fishing. Winter schools often hold deeper, which can limit shore reach. These moderate monthly judgments use the established local fishery and species behavior; the actual bank depth, fish size and current catch rate remain variable.

name: Simpson Street Slough launch
waterSpeedNote: Slow near-bank drift is inferred at the selected access. This describes the fishing margin; stronger flow farther out is not a second water-speed category.
description: A small public launch on slow water. Crappie and bass offer a modest fishing possibility, with a strict resident-fish meal limit and little open bank.

scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: the documented Simpson entry reaches a wooded slough corridor, giving some screening from neighboring industrial yards. The small dock remains shared with paddlers, and anyone using that approach can see the fishing position.
scoreReasons.bankQuantity: One launch opening supplies most of the casting area; adjacent banks are wooded or private.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Open casting lanes exist at the chosen entry; the description identifies vegetation and footing limits.
scoreReasons.accessEase: Use lawful street parking at the documented 11198 NE Simpson entrance. Enter the public launch corridor beside the natural area, passing the cable and keeping left of the mound toward the dock. Do not enter the neighboring industrial yards.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: The Slough is explicitly described as slow water; a simple float or light bottom rig is workable here.
scoreReasons.scenery: The rating reflects the visible river, trees and surrounding development.
scoreReasons.evidence: Manager access information, the fishing inventory and inspected imagery support this candidate. Its scores remain judgments that can change with experience.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Spring and fall can draw crappie into reachable cover and support useful bank fishing. Winter schools often hold deeper, which can limit shore reach. name: Sauvie Island Ferry Road ramp
waterSpeedNote: Slow near-bank drift is inferred at the selected access. This describes the fishing margin; stronger flow farther out is not a second water-speed category.
description: A compact free public ramp on the Multnomah Channel. It works for a quick bank session, especially when the boat lane is quiet.

scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The fishing margin shares the ramp opening with launch users and is beside a road-end lot and residential moorage. Trees around the property offer limited screening at the water itself, and the compact public corridor leaves little room to hide from view.
scoreReasons.bankQuantity: The ramp and its immediate edge are the usable public fishing area.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Open casting lanes exist at the chosen entry; the description identifies vegetation and footing limits.

scoreReasons.waterManageability: The sheltered channel margin is generally manageable with light weight, though tides and passing boats move the line.
scoreReasons.scenery: The rating reflects the visible river, trees and surrounding development.
scoreReasons.evidence: Manager access information, the fishing inventory and inspected imagery support this candidate. Its scores remain judgments that can change with experience.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Spring and autumn salmon migrations provide the strongest dinner rationale. Summer crappie add a limited alternative under the resident-fish meal advisory.

scoreReasons.bankQuality: Roots, vegetation, rocks or a sloping edge restrict some casting angles.

scoreReasons.bankQuality: The selected gravel bar is clear enough for ordinary lure casts.
scoreReasons.accessEase: A gated access road requires about a quarter-mile walk.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: The downstream bank margin is softer than the main chute, but this is a moving gorge river.
scoreReasons.scenery: Open gravel, a forested canyon and a wild river.
scoreReasons.evidence: BLM day-use authorization and the Marine Board access point agree; imagery shows the gravel bank.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Fall salmon and winter steelhead create seasonal opportunities. High runoff reduces the available gravel and makes float control harder.

name: Punchbowl Falls Park · confluence beach
waterSpeedNote: The selected West Fork-side eddy is sheltered from the East Fork rapid.
description: A spectacular confluence reached by a forest trail. Work the quiet West Fork edge well below the falls deadline.

scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The forested canyon and descent put the confluence beach out of ordinary road and park-lawn view. Trees and terrain screen the approach, while the open gravel beach is still shared with hikers, swimmers and other anglers.
scoreReasons.bankQuantity: A useful cobble beach sits at the confluence, with steep canyon walls elsewhere.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Open cobble allows short casts; the water edge shifts.
scoreReasons.accessEase: A roughly mile-long trail includes steep boulder steps near the beach.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: The lower West Fork has an eddy at the beach; the East Fork rapid is much faster.
scoreReasons.scenery: A dramatic wooded confluence below basalt cliffs.
scoreReasons.evidence: County access, trail descriptions and the exact angling deadline are well documented.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Winter steelhead and spring hatchery Chinook are the strongest run-based prospects. Fall coho remain a possibility. High water can submerge the beach.

name: Kingsley Reservoir · day-use bank
waterSpeedNote: Still reservoir water; wind may create chop.
description: A stocked forest reservoir with room to spread out. It sits near the two-hour edge, and late-season drawdown changes the bank.

scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: the selected Kingsley bank has a band of trees between portions of the road and shoreline. Its closeness to the dam and day-use approach leaves intermittent sightlines from walkers, launch visitors and other anglers despite room to spread out.
scoreReasons.bankQuantity: Open reservoir edges provide many fishing positions when water is reachable.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Open banks permit ordinary casts; drawdown can leave soft footing.
scoreReasons.accessEase: Day-use parking is near the reservoir, with a short sloping walk.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: Still reservoir water suits bait and spinners.
scoreReasons.scenery: A forested mountain reservoir with broad open views.
scoreReasons.evidence: County stocking confirmation, public access and Marine Board status provide strong support.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Spring stocking and early summer are strongest. October cooling can help trout, while irrigation drawdown can make bank access muddy or distant. Winter snow often limits access.

name: East Pond at Klineline · south bank
generalAreaName: East Pond, Salmon Creek Regional Park
waterSpeedNote: Small pond water should permit simple bait, bobber and spinner presentations. This classification describes the pond side of the dike. Salmon Creek runs alongside the approach and has its own flow and fishing rules.
description: Small pond east of I-5 with a park trail along its southern bank. Historical catches favor bluegill and small largemouth bass. Keeper potential for your preferred species is limited; current-season prospects remain unknown.

scoreReasons.seclusion: Judgment: The longer walk beyond Klineline reduces casual fishing traffic, and trees provide some screening around the pond. The selected south-bank dike is also the walking route, with an open waterside strip and nearby road-facing gaps, so passing walkers can easily see an angler.
scoreReasons.bankQuantity: Judgment: the southern dike and portions of the eastern margin provide a substantial accessible stretch. Vegetation narrows some openings. The county map and aerial support the south-bank approach.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: Judgment: the selected grassy shoreline has open water in front and room for ordinary casts. A narrow unpaved edge and changing vegetation require care when landing fish.
scoreReasons.accessEase: Judgment: a straightforward park walk with two footbridges and a freeway underpass. The final section is an unpaved dike trail. Walking time is estimated at 10-15 minutes.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: Judgment: this small stillwater pond should allow a beginner to hold bait and a bobber in place and retrieve a spinner without fighting river current.
scoreReasons.scenery: Judgment: an attractive small pond with trees and birds, bordered by visible roads and development. an angler described it as pretty while driving past on October 30, 2026.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: Current keeper prospects for trout, smallmouth, salmon, crappie or useful perch remain unknown. Historical reports support bluegill and small largemouth bass. The East-coded trout records end in 2012 and their geographic match needs confirmation.
scoreReasons.evidence: Strong public ownership, trail and physical-layout evidence. Fishing evidence consists of old angler accounts and historical East-coded trout plants with an unresolved geographic crosswalk.

name: Grays River · Covered Bridge north bank
generalAreaName: Grays River Covered Bridge / Ahlberg Park
waterSpeedNote: The selected shore entry reaches the shallow margin beside the north gravel bank. Slow is a bank-margin inference from the viewed layout and July 2025 photograph. The main channel can run strongly; an October 2015 paddler struggled against it. Rain can cover the exposed gravel and remove the manageable edge.
description: A short dirt path reaches the gravel bank beside the historic covered bridge. The north-bank owner permits public use; Ahlberg Park is across the bridge. Open gravel provides room to cast, with clear sightlines from the bridge and nearby approach.

scoreReasons.seclusion: The bridge and approach overlook much of the gravel. Trees screen parts of the path and inland views, while anglers remain visible to bridge visitors and people across the river.
scoreReasons.bankQuantity: A broad gravel edge extends downstream from the short access path in low to moderate water. Higher river levels can sharply reduce the available dry bank.
scoreReasons.bankQuality: The gravel offers open casting angles with little immediate overhead cover. Stay clear of the bridge, swimmers and launching paddlers.
scoreReasons.accessEase: The north turnout and river entry are close together. The approach is unpaved with loose stones and an uneven slope, requiring about 1-3 minutes on foot.
scoreReasons.waterManageability: The accessible shallow edge allows short controlled presentations in ordinary water. Stronger channel flow and rain-driven rises reduce the usable margin.
scoreReasons.scenery: The historic timber bridge, wooded hills and open river valley make this a particularly scenic access.
scoreReasons.evidence: Dated local public-access reporting, recent ground photographs, aerial inspection and current river rules support the location. Recent bank catch rates and present river level remain unknown.
scoreReasons.seasonalProspects: November offers a legal hatchery-salmon opportunity in established salmon habitat. Meal-size wild trout must be released, and the 2021 hatchery change limits reliance on older stocking claims. A 5 reflects a plausible, selective keeper fishery with modest present support.

parking.label: North-side gravel turnout beside Covered Bridge Road
parking.notes: Use the existing gravel pull-off, keeping the road and water-access track clear. Public use rests on landowner permission described in September 2026 local reporting.

fishing.notes: The point is at the dry bank approach above the gravel margin. Choose exposed stable gravel along the waterline; river level changes the usable standing position.

visualVerification.method: November 1, 2026 Esri World Imagery inspection with returned image bounds, separate centered pin checks, July 2025 ground photograph and supplied satellite screenshot.
visualVerification.notes: The north gravel turnout connects to a short track down to the bank without crossing the bridge or a residential yard. The ground photograph confirms a walkable gravel margin. Aerial and photograph dates differ, and neither establishes current water height.

walk.description: From the north turnout, follow the short dirt track toward the river just west of the bridge. Descend onto exposed gravel at the shore entry. The surface is uneven and can be muddy or submerged after rain.

accessNotes: The north bank is privately owned land with documented public permission. Keep the turnout and launch approach clear, stay on the established access and bank, and respect any newer posted restriction. Ahlberg Park occupies the south side. The north route avoids crossing the single-lane bridge.

currentStatus.label: Public-permission bank access
currentStatus.summary: September 17, 2026 reporting confirms continued public permission on the north end. November 1 review found a connected turnout-to-bank route and a legal mainstem hatchery-salmon season.

retentionNotes: This bank is in WAC 220-312-030(25)(b), between Barr Road Bridge downstream and Highway 4 Bridge upstream. Mainstem Grays River is open from the Saturday before Memorial Day through March 15 under the current southwest rules. August 1-December 31 salmon limit is six, up to two adults; retain hatchery Chinook and hatchery coho only. Chinook require an adipose and/or ventral fin clip. Release cutthroat and wild rainbow trout. Night closure, anti-snagging and stationary-gear restrictions apply August 1-November 15; January 1-March 15 has selective-gear rules with barbed hooks allowed. Current statewide license, size and catch-record requirements also apply. The installed-weir closure in subsection (c) concerns the reach upstream of Highway 4. The October 29, 2026 agency table reports both Grays weirs removed.
seasonNotes: Autumn salmon provide the clearest keeper rationale. Winter steelhead are present in the watershed, with hatchery availability less certain following the 2021 hatchery change. The mainstem closes March 16 through the Friday before Memorial Day. The seasonal calendar is a judgment about retained fish from the bank.
crowdNotes: A known sightseeing and swimming stop. The open bridge and approach create visibility even with few anglers. Summer swimmers, paddlers and events can concentrate use; no measured current crowd count is available.
unknowns: Current water height and the extent of exposed gravel.
Recent bank catch rates and the proportion of available fish eligible for retention.
Any newer on-site restriction than the dated public-permission report.

Wild trout release rules and the March 16 to late-May closure limit the remainder of the year. These scores are practical judgments about the retained-fish opportunity.

availability.reason: 2026-11-01: Dated local reporting confirms the north-end landowner permits public use. Aerial and ground images support the turnout-to-bank route. Current mainstem rules permit a hatchery-salmon opportunity; October 29 agency reporting lists both Grays weirs removed.

overallReason: Good usable bank, short access and scenery, with moderate privacy and a selective seasonal keeper opportunity.

accessAudit.summary: The north turnout connects by a short dirt track to a visible gravel bank. September 2026 local reporting identifies the private owner and continued public permission; the 2021 visitor guide explicitly includes fishing on both sides.
findings: North-side public permission is documented separately from the south-side park.
The existing gravel pull-off and river track are visible in aerial imagery.
The July 2025 ground photograph shows a usable gravel bank beside the bridge.
High water can cover the gravel; the pin marks the shore entry above its changing edge.
County atlas pages 14-15 place the bridge between Barr Road and Highway 4, within the mainstem regulation subsection (25)(b).

limitations: Current occupancy and seasonal vegetation vary.
Farther downstream bank ownership and access were not extended beyond the documented bridge access.
privacyReview.physicalSpaceReason: The exposed gravel offers several separated casting positions in ordinary water. High water reduces that room.

fishingBackground: Agency monitoring documents salmon and steelhead habitat at the bridge. The legal keeper target is chiefly hatchery salmon during the open season. The local hatchery ceased production in 2021, so old stocking-based recommendations require fresh release-location evidence.
